Strong qq-log-convexity of the dd-Hoggatt polynomials

Shane Chern S. ChernFakultät für Mathematik, Universität Wien, Oskar-Morgenstern-Platz 1, Wien 1090, Austria Email address: chenxiaohang92@gmail.com, xiaohangc92@univie.ac.at and Wenle Shi W. ShiSchool of Mathematical Sciences, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian 116024, P.R. China Email address: shi-wenle@hotmail.com
Abstract.

In this paper, three (qq-)log-convexity or concavity properties related to the dd-Hoggatt numbers are investigated. First, we show that the dd-Hoggatt transformation preserves the log-convexity of a sequence. We then establish the strong qq-log-concavity of a qq-analog of dd-Hoggatt numbers. Finally, we prove the core result of this work, namely, the sequence of dd-Hoggatt polynomials is strongly qq-log-convex, based on the theory of Schur functions.

Key words and phrases: 
dd-Hoggatt number, dd-Hoggatt polynomial, dd-Hoggatt transform, qq-log-convexity, qq-log-concavity, Schur positivity.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
05E05, 05A05, 05A20.

1. Introduction

Given a sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} of nonnegative real numbers, we say it is log-concave if the inequality

an2≥an−1​an+1\displaystyle a_{n}^{2}\geq a_{n-1}a_{n+1}

holds for all n≥1n\geq 1, and log-convex if

an−1​an+1≥an2.\displaystyle a_{n-1}a_{n+1}\geq a_{n}^{2}.

If we lift elements in the sequence to polynomials in ℝ⁡[q]\mathbb{R}[q] with qq an indeterminate and define the qq-analog of the order relation “≥\geq” by f(q)≥qg(q)f(q)\geq_{q}g(q) provided that f⁡(q)−g⁡(q)∈ℝ≥0​[q]f(q)-g(q)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}[q], then the concept of log-concavity and log-convexity is naturally extended to qq-log-concavity and qq-log-convexity. Sagan [13, p. 290] further introduced the nontion of strong qq-log-concavity: a sequence (an​(q))n≥0(a_{n}(q))_{n\geq 0} of polynomials over ℝ\mathbb{R} is strongly qq-log-concave if

an(q)am(q)≥qan+1(q)am−1(q)\displaystyle a_{n}(q)a_{m}(q)\geq_{q}a_{n+1}(q)a_{m-1}(q)

for all n≥m≥1n\geq m\geq 1. In the same vein, we say the sequence (an​(q))n≥0(a_{n}(q))_{n\geq 0} is strongly qq-log-convex if

an+1(q)am−1(q)≥qan(q)am(q).\displaystyle a_{n+1}(q)a_{m-1}(q)\geq_{q}a_{n}(q)a_{m}(q).

In particular, for ordinary qq-log-concavity and qq-log-convexity, we only require the two inequalities for the case where mm and nn are equal.

Inspired by a conjecture of Verner Hoggatt in private communication, Fielder and Alford [8, Section 4] introduced the dd-Hoggatt triangle (⟨nk⟩(d))0≤k≤n\big({\textstyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{(d)}\big)_{0\leq k\leq n}, which specializes to the Pascal triangle ((nk))0≤k≤n\big(\binom{n}{k}\big)_{0\leq k\leq n} at d=1d=1. The original definition of Fielder and Alford [8, p. 163, eq. (13)] is recursive. However, it is easy to derive the following product formula in terms of binomial coefficients from their recurrence relation:

⟨nk⟩=⟨nk⟩(d):=∏j=0n−1(n+jk)(k+jk),\displaystyle{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}={\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{(d)}:=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\binom{n+j}{k}}{\binom{k+j}{k}}, (1.1)

valid for n,k≥0n,k\geq 0. It is known that the 22- and 33-Hoggatt triangles are the Narayana triangle [14, Entry A001263] and the Baxter triangle [14, Entry A056939], respectively.

For a triangular array of combinatorial numbers (Sn,k)0≤k≤n(S_{n,k})_{0\leq k\leq n}, we define a linear transformation that maps a sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} to a new sequence (cn)n≥0(c_{n})_{n\geq 0} by

cn=∑k=0nSn,k​ak.\displaystyle c_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}S_{n,k}a_{k}.

We know from the Davenport–Pólya theorem [7, p. 1, Theorem 2] that if the sequences (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} and (bn)n≥0(b_{n})_{n\geq 0} are log-convex, then so is their binomial convolution

cn=∑k=0n(nk)​ak​bn−k.\displaystyle c_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}a_{k}b_{n-k}.

Motivated by this phenomenon, Liu and Wang [10, p. 474, Conjecture 5.2] conjectured that the Narayana transformation also preserves the log-convexity. This prediction was later confirmed by Chen, Wang, and Yang [3, p. 318, Theorem 4.3]. Quite recently, Liu and Mao [11, Theorem 6.1] further discovered the same behavior of the Baxter transformation. In this work, we provide a unified treatment on the generic dd-Hoggatt transformation.

Theorem 1.1.

Let d≥1d\geq 1 be fixed. If the sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} of nonnegative real numbers is log-convex, then so is the sequence (cn)n≥0(c_{n})_{n\geq 0} where

cn=∑k=0n⟨nk⟩(d)​ak.\displaystyle c_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{(d)}a_{k}.

Note that in the proof of the Narayana case, the basic idea of Chen, Wang, and Yang builds on the strong qq-log-convexity of the Narayana polynomials [3, p. 311, Theorem 3.2], the weaker version of which was first conjectured by Liu and Wang [10, p. 474, Conjecture 5.1]. Later on, Zhu [16, p. 605, Proposition 3.20] offered an alternative proof of this strong qq-log-convexity. For Baxter polynomials, we recently witnessed their strong qq-log-convexity in the work of Liu and Mao [11, Theorem 5.1]. Now let us define the dd-Hoggatt polynomials by

Hn​(q)=Hn(d)​(q):=∑k=0n⟨nk⟩(d)​qk.\displaystyle H_{n}(q)=H^{(d)}_{n}(q):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{(d)}q^{k}.

Mao and the second author [12, p. 17] conjectured that (Hn(d)​(q))n≥0\big(H^{(d)}_{n}(q)\big)_{n\geq 0} is qq-log-convex for fixed d≥1d\geq 1. Here we not only provide an affirmative answer to this problem but also establish a strengthening toward strong qq-log-convexity, which will serve as an essential tool in our proof of Theorem 1.1. This is also the most central result of the present work.

Theorem 1.2.

Let d≥1d\geq 1 be fixed. The sequence (Hn(d)​(q))n≥0\big(H^{(d)}_{n}(q)\big)_{n\geq 0} is strongly qq-log-convex.

Cigler [6] recently considered a qq-analog of the dd-Hoggatt numbers:11 1 We multiply the original definition of Cigler [6, p. 10, eq. (22)] by the prefactor qd​(k2)q^{d\binom{k}{2}}. This is consistent with Cigler’s remark on [6, p. 14] and the qq-Narayana numbers studied by Chen, Wang, and Yang [3, p. 306].

⟨nk⟩q=⟨nk⟩q(d):=qd​(k2)​∏j=0d−1[n+jk]q[k+jk]q,\displaystyle{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}={\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{(d)}_{q}:=q^{d\binom{k}{2}}\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n+j}{k}}_{q}}{{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{k+j}{k}}_{q}}, (1.2)

where the qq-binomial coefficients are given by

[nk]q:=[n]q![k]q!​[n−k]q!,\displaystyle{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}:=\frac{[n]_{q}!}{[k]_{q}![n-k]_{q}!},

with

[m]q:=1−qm1−q,[m]q!:=[1]q[2]q⋯[m]q.\displaystyle[m]_{q}:=\frac{1-q^{m}}{1-q},\qquad\qquad[m]_{q}!:=[1]_{q}[2]_{q}\cdots[m]_{q}.

For the sequence ([nk]q)0≤k≤n\big({\textstyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}\big)_{0\leq k\leq n} of qq-binomial coefficients with nn fixed, its strong qq-log-concavity was shown by Butler [2, p. 59, Theorem 4.2] and Sagan [13, p. 292, Theorem 2.3]. Simultaneously, Butler [2, p. 62, Section 5] proved that the sequence ([nk]q)n≥k\big({\textstyle\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}\big)_{n\geq k} with kk fixed is strongly qq-log-concave via a partition-theoretic approach and Sagan [13, p. 297, Corollary 3.4(2)] provided another proof by the theory of symmetric functions. Around the same time, Krattenthaler [9, p. 334, Theorem 1], independently, established an even stronger result that for n≥m≥0n\geq m\geq 0 and k≥l≥0k\geq l\geq 0,

[nl]q[mk]q≥q[nl−1]q[mk+1]q.\displaystyle{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{l}}_{q}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{m}{k}}_{q}\geq_{q}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{l-1}}_{q}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{m}{k+1}}_{q}.

A parallel inequality

[nl]q[mk]q≥q[n+1l]q[m−1k]q,\displaystyle{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{l}}_{q}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{m}{k}}_{q}\geq_{q}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n+1}{l}}_{q}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{m-1}{k}}_{q},

valid for nonnegative integers n,m,l,kn,m,l,k with k≥lk\geq l and n+k≥m+ln+k\geq m+l, was discovered by the first author [4, p. 34, Theorem 1.3]. Moving forward to the qq-Narayana numbers, a similar strong qq-log-concavity property was discovered by Chen, Wang, and Yang [3, p. 320, Theorem 5.2 and p. 323, Theorem 5.6] for fixed nn or fixed kk. Recently, Liu and Mao [11, Theorems 6.6 and 6.7] further proved that for d≥1d\geq 1, the qq-analog ⟨nk⟩q(d){\textstyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{(d)}_{q} of the dd-Hoggatt numbers is qq-log-concave for fixed nn or fixed kk. In this work, we strengthen this discovery to strong qq-log-concavity.

Theorem 1.3.

Let d≥1d\geq 1 and n≥0n\geq 0 be fixed. The sequence (⟨nk⟩q(d))0≤k≤n\big({\textstyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{(d)}_{q}\big)_{0\leq k\leq n} is strongly qq-log-concave.

Theorem 1.4.

Let d≥1d\geq 1 and k≥0k\geq 0 be fixed. The sequence (⟨nk⟩q(d))n≥k\big({\textstyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{(d)}_{q}\big)_{n\geq k} is strongly qq-log-concave.

Outline of the paper. In Section 2, we study the dd-Hoggatt transformation and prove Theorem 1.1 under the assumption of Theorem 1.2. We then collect some preliminary results in Section 3 on the theory of symmetric functions, especially of Schur functions. Building on these results, we demonstrate Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 in Section 4. Finally, we move on to the most difficult task in this work, namely, showing the strong qq-log-convexity of the dd-Hoggatt polynomials. To begin with, we establish the Schur positivity of an auxiliary family of functions in Section 5. Then Theorem 1.2 will be established in Section 6.

In subsequent sections, we always fix d≥1d\geq 1 and omit the superscript “(d)(d)” if the value of dd does not interfere with our analysis.

2. dd-Hoggatt transformation

In this section, we show that the dd-Hoggatt transformation preserves the log-convexity. To begin with, we require the Pochhammer symbols for m∈ℕ∪{∞}m\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}:

(x)m:=∏k=0m−1(x+k).\displaystyle(x)_{m}:=\prod_{k=0}^{m-1}(x+k).

It is clear from (1.1) that

⟨n+1k⟩⟨nk⟩=(n+1)d(n−k+1)d,⟨n−1k⟩⟨nk⟩=(n−k)d(n)d.\displaystyle\frac{{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+1}{k}}}{{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}}=\frac{(n+1)_{d}}{(n-k+1)_{d}},\qquad\qquad\frac{{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}}}{{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}}=\frac{(n-k)_{d}}{(n)_{d}}. (2.1)

For n≥1n\geq 1, 0≤r≤2​n0\leq r\leq 2n, and 0≤k≤⌊r2⌋0\leq k\leq\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor, let us define

αk​(n,r):={⟨n+1k⟩​⟨n−1r−k⟩+⟨n+1r−k⟩​⟨n−1k⟩−2​⟨nk⟩​⟨nr−k⟩,if k<r2,⟨n+1k⟩​⟨n−1k⟩−⟨nk⟩2,if k=r2.\displaystyle\alpha_{k}(n,r):=\begin{cases}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+1}{k}}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{r-k}}+{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+1}{r-k}}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}}-2{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{r-k}},&\text{if $k<\frac{r}{2}$},\\[6.0pt] {\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+1}{k}}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}}-{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{2},&\text{if $k=\frac{r}{2}$}.\end{cases} (2.2)

It is simple to verify that

Hn−1​(q)​Hn+1​(q)−Hn​(q)2=∑r=02​n∑k=0⌊r2⌋αk​(n,r)​qr.\displaystyle H_{n-1}(q)H_{n+1}(q)-H_{n}(q)^{2}=\sum_{r=0}^{2n}\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor}\alpha_{k}(n,r)q^{r}.

In view of the qq-log-convexity of (Hn​(q))n≥0(H_{n}(q))_{n\geq 0} stated in Theorem 1.2,

Hn−1​(q)​Hn+1​(q)−Hn​(q)2∈ℕ⁡[q],\displaystyle H_{n-1}(q)H_{n+1}(q)-H_{n}(q)^{2}\in\mathbb{N}[q],

we know that

∑k=0⌊r2⌋αk​(n,r)≥0.\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor}\alpha_{k}(n,r)\geq 0. (2.3)

Therefore, if we fix n≥1n\geq 1 and 0≤r≤2​n0\leq r\leq 2n, then it is impossible that αk​(n,r)<0\alpha_{k}(n,r)<0 for every kk with 0≤k≤⌊r2⌋0\leq k\leq\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor. In what follows, we characterize the sign change of αk​(n,r)\alpha_{k}(n,r).

Lemma 2.1.

For given n≥1n\geq 1 and 0≤r≤2​n0\leq r\leq 2n, there exists an integer k′:=k′​(n,r)k^{\prime}:=k^{\prime}(n,r) such that

αk​(n,r)​{≥0,when 0≤k≤k′,≤0,when k′<k≤⌊r2⌋.\displaystyle\alpha_{k}(n,r)\begin{cases}\geq 0,&\text{when $0\leq k\leq k^{\prime}$},\\ \leq 0,&\text{when $k^{\prime}<k\leq\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor$}.\end{cases}
Proof.

Throughout, we always assume k≥0k\geq 0. We start by noticing that

αk​(n,r)​{=0,when k≤r−n−2,>0,when k=r−n−1.\displaystyle\alpha_{k}(n,r)\begin{cases}=0,&\text{when $k\leq r-n-2$},\\ >0,&\text{when $k=r-n-1$}.\end{cases}

For the first situation, we use the fact that ⟨n−1r−k⟩=⟨nr−k⟩=⟨n+1r−k⟩=0{\textstyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{r-k}}={\textstyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{r-k}}={\textstyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+1}{r-k}}=0 when k≤r−n−2k\leq r-n-2. For the second situation, we note that k≠r2k\neq\frac{r}{2} and k≤n−1k\leq n-1 because r≤2​nr\leq 2n. Thus, αk​(n,r)=⟨n−1k⟩>0\alpha_{k}(n,r)={\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}}>0. In the sequel, suppose k≥r−nk\geq r-n. Let us introduce an auxiliary sequence indexed by kk:

βk​(n,r):=(n−k)d(n−r+k+1)d+(n−r+k)d(n−k+1)d.\displaystyle\beta_{k}(n,r):=\frac{(n-k)_{d}}{(n-r+k+1)_{d}}+\frac{(n-r+k)_{d}}{(n-k+1)_{d}}.

In light of (2.1),

n+dn​βk​(n,r)−2={1⟨nk⟩​⟨nr−k⟩​αk​(n,r),if k≤r2,2⟨nk⟩2​αk​(n,r),if k=r2.\displaystyle\frac{n+d}{n}\beta_{k}(n,r)-2=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{r-k}}}\alpha_{k}(n,r),&\text{if $k\leq\frac{r}{2}$},\\[10.0pt] \frac{2}{{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{2}}\alpha_{k}(n,r),&\text{if $k=\frac{r}{2}$}.\end{cases}

For consecutive indices k,k+1k,k+1 satisfying k≥r−nk\geq r-n and k+1≤⌊r2⌋k+1\leq\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor, we have

n−k>n−r+k+1≥1,\displaystyle n-k>n-r+k+1\geq 1,

so that

(n−k)d−1​(n−k)d+1≥(n−r+k+1)d−1​(n−r+k+1)d+1,\displaystyle(n-k)_{d-1}(n-k)_{d+1}\geq(n-r+k+1)_{d-1}(n-r+k+1)_{d+1},

which further gives us the nonnegativity of

βk​(n,r)−βk+1​(n,r)=d⁡(2​n−r+d)​((n−k)d−1(n−r+k+1)d+1−(n−r+k+1)d−1(n−k)d+1).\displaystyle\beta_{k}(n,r)-\beta_{k+1}(n,r)=d(2n-r+d)\left(\frac{(n-k)_{d-1}}{(n-r+k+1)_{d+1}}-\frac{(n-r+k+1)_{d-1}}{(n-k)_{d+1}}\right).

Thus, the numbers βk​(n,r)\beta_{k}(n,r) are nonincreasing in kk, and so are n+dn​βk​(n,r)−2\frac{n+d}{n}\beta_{k}(n,r)-2. We conclude that when kk runs from 00 to ⌊r2⌋\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor, the sign of αk​(n,r)\alpha_{k}(n,r) changes at most once, from nonnegative to nonpositive. The claimed characterization then follows. ∎

Now we are in a position to prove Theorem 1.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Note that

cn−1​cn+1−cn2=∑r=02​n∑k=0⌊r2⌋αk​(n,r)​ak​ar−k.\displaystyle c_{n-1}c_{n+1}-c_{n}^{2}=\sum_{r=0}^{2n}\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor}\alpha_{k}(n,r)a_{k}a_{r-k}.

Since (ak)k≥0(a_{k})_{k\geq 0} is a log-convex sequence of nonnegative real numbers, we obtain that

a0​ar≥a1​ar−1≥⋯≥a⌊r2⌋​ar−⌊r2⌋≥0.\displaystyle a_{0}a_{r}\geq a_{1}a_{r-1}\geq\cdots\geq a_{\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor}a_{r-\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor}\geq 0.

Now choosing k′k^{\prime} as in Lemma 2.1, we see that for every kk with 0≤k≤⌊r2⌋0\leq k\leq\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor,

αk​(n,r)​(ak​ar−k−ak′​ar−k′)≥0.\displaystyle\alpha_{k}(n,r)(a_{k}a_{r-k}-a_{k^{\prime}}a_{r-k^{\prime}})\geq 0.

Therefore,

∑k=0⌊r2⌋αk​(n,r)​ak​ar−k=ak′​ar−k′​∑k=0⌊r2⌋αk​(n,r)+∑k=0⌊r2⌋αk​(n,r)​(ak​ar−k−ak′​ar−k′)≥0,\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor}\alpha_{k}(n,r)a_{k}a_{r-k}=a_{k^{\prime}}a_{r-k^{\prime}}\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor}\alpha_{k}(n,r)+\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{r}{2}\rfloor}\alpha_{k}(n,r)(a_{k}a_{r-k}-a_{k^{\prime}}a_{r-k^{\prime}})\geq 0,

where we have recalled (2.3) for the nonnegativity of the first sum. Summing over rr gives the desired log-convexity of cnc_{n}. ∎

3. Preliminaries on Schur functions

In this section, we give a brief overview of the theory of Schur functions, most of which can be found in the monograph of Stanley [15, Chapter 7].

We begin with the combinatorial setting. A partition is a weakly decreasing sequence λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λl)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{l}) of positive integers. If the sequence is empty, we say this partition is the empty partition ∅\varnothing. We write |λ||\lambda| for its size ∑i=1lλi\sum_{i=1}^{l}\lambda_{i}. Also, the length of λ\lambda, denoted by 𝗅𝖾𝗇⁡(λ)\mathsf{len}(\lambda), is defined as ll, and the width is defined as λ1\lambda_{1}. When an index ii exceeds the length of λ\lambda, the corresponding part λi\lambda_{i} is understood to be 00. The Young diagram of λ\lambda is obtained by depicting left-aligned boxes in rows such that there are λi\lambda_{i} boxes in the ii-th row. By flipping the Young diagram along the main diagonal, we obtain the Young diagram of a new partition, which is called the conjugate of λ\lambda, denoted by λ𝖳\lambda^{\mathsf{T}}. For two partitions μ\mu and λ\lambda, the notation μ⊆λ\mu\subseteq\lambda means μi≤λi\mu_{i}\leq\lambda_{i} for every index ii. The skew diagram λ/μ\lambda/\mu is obtained by removing the Young diagram of μ\mu from the upper-left corner of the diagram of λ\lambda. We also write (λ/μ)𝖳:=λ𝖳/μ𝖳(\lambda/\mu)^{\mathsf{T}}:=\lambda^{\mathsf{T}}/\mu^{\mathsf{T}}.

Assuming μ⊆λ\mu\subseteq\lambda, a semistandard Young tableau of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a filling TT of the cells in the skew diagram of λ/μ\lambda/\mu by positive integers that is weakly increasing from left to right in every row and strictly increasing from top to bottom in every column. Its type is the sequence (m1,m2,…)(m_{1},m_{2},\ldots), where mim_{i} denotes the multiplicity of ii in the filling TT. Let X:=(x1,x2,…)X:=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots) be a list of variables, known as an alphabet, and put

XT:=∏i≥1ximi.\displaystyle X^{T}:=\prod_{i\geq 1}x_{i}^{m_{i}}.

The combinatorial definition of the skew Schur function indexed by λ/μ\lambda/\mu is [15, p. 310, Definition 7.10.1]:

sλ/μ=sλ/μ​(X):=∑TXT,\displaystyle s_{\lambda/\mu}=s_{\lambda/\mu}(X):=\sum_{T}X^{T},

summing over all semistandard Young tableaux of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu. For μ=∅\mu=\varnothing, we have the ordinary Schur function sλ=sλ​(X)s_{\lambda}=s_{\lambda}(X). We also use the convention sλ/μ=0s_{\lambda/\mu}=0 if μ⊈λ\mu\not\subseteq\lambda.

Schur functions play a central role in the theory of symmetric functions. Let Λ\Lambda be the ring of symmetric functions over ℤ\mathbb{Z}. An important fact is that the Schur functions sλs_{\lambda} form a basis for Λ\Lambda; see [15, p. 315, Corollary 7.10.6]. Moreover, this basis is orthogonal, given by the Hall inner product [15, p. 336]:

⟨sλ,sμ⟩={1,if λ=μ,0,if λ≠μ.\displaystyle\big\langle s_{\lambda},s_{\mu}\big\rangle=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if $\lambda=\mu$},\\ 0,&\text{if $\lambda\neq\mu$}.\end{cases}

Let F=∑λaλ​sλ∈ΛF=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}s_{\lambda}\in\Lambda be arbitrary, expanded by the Schur basis. We write

[sλ]​F:=aλ=⟨sλ,F⟩.\displaystyle[s_{\lambda}]F:=a_{\lambda}=\big\langle s_{\lambda},F\big\rangle.

If [sλ]​F≥0[s_{\lambda}]F\geq 0 for every partition λ\lambda, then we say FF is Schur positive, expressed by F≥s0F\geq_{s}0.

We know from [15, p. 338, eq. (7.64)] that

sμ​sν\displaystyle s_{\mu}s_{\nu} =∑λcμ,νλ​sλ,\displaystyle=\sum_{\lambda}c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}s_{\lambda}, (3.1)
sλ/ν\displaystyle s_{\lambda/\nu} =∑μcμ,νλ​sμ,\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu}c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}s_{\mu}, (3.2)
sλ/μ\displaystyle s_{\lambda/\mu} =∑νcμ,νλ​sν,\displaystyle=\sum_{\nu}c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}s_{\nu}, (3.3)

using the same Littlewood–Richardson coefficients cμ,νλc_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}. In particular, for arbitrary F∈ΛF\in\Lambda,

⟨sλ/μ,F⟩=⟨sλ,sμ​F⟩,\displaystyle\big\langle s_{\lambda/\mu},F\big\rangle=\big\langle s_{\lambda},s_{\mu}F\big\rangle, (3.4)

both equal to ∑ν(cμ,νλ⋅[sν]​F)\sum_{\nu}\big(c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}\cdot[s_{\nu}]F\big).

To further understand the Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, we require the Littlewood–Richardson rule. We first obtain the reverse row word of a tableau by reading each row from right to left, beginning with the top row and then proceeding downward. Moreover, a word is a lattice word if in every initial segment, the multiplicity of ii is at least the multiplicity of i+1i+1 for every i≥1i\geq 1. Now a Littlewood–Richardson tableau is a semistandard Young tableau whose reverse row word is a lattice word. It follows from this definition that the type of a Littlewood–Richardson tableau forms a partition.

The Littlewood–Richardson rule [15, p. 432, Theorem A1.3.3] states that cμ,νλc_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda} equals the number of Littlewood–Richardson tableaux of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu and type ν\nu, yielding that cμ,νλ≥0c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}\geq 0, and hence that

  1. (1)

    Every skew Schur function is Schur positive;

  2. (2)

    A product of Schur positive symmetric functions is Schur positive.

We collect some additional facts about the Littlewood–Richardson tableaux and coefficients.

Lemma 3.1.

Every entry in the ii-th row of a Littlewood–Richardson tableau is no larger than ii. Also, if cμ,νλ>0c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}>0, then μ,ν⊆λ\mu,\nu\subseteq\lambda and for every i≥1i\geq 1,

λi≤μ1+νi.\displaystyle\lambda_{i}\leq\mu_{1}+\nu_{i}. (3.5)
Proof.

We prove the first assertion inductively on ii. For the first row, the rightmost cell must be filled with 11 by the Littlewood–Richardson condition, and hence all entries in this row are 11 by weak monotonicity. Suppose all entries in rows above the ii-th row are at most i−1i-1. Then the rightmost entry in the ii-th row cannot exceed ii; otherwise, the Littlewood–Richardson condition is violated at this cell. We then conclude that all entries in this row are at most ii by weak monotonicity.

For the second assertion, since cμ,νλ>0c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}>0, we have at least one Littlewood–Richardson tableau of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu and type ν\nu. Then μ⊆λ\mu\subseteq\lambda from the shape. Meanwhile, in (3.1), switching μ\mu and ν\nu does not change the left-hand side but turns cμ,νλc_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda} to cν,μλc_{\nu,\mu}^{\lambda} on the right-hand side. Thus,

cμ,νλ=cν,μλ.\displaystyle c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}=c_{\nu,\mu}^{\lambda}.

Then ν⊆λ\nu\subseteq\lambda is also true. Next, if λi≤μ1\lambda_{i}\leq\mu_{1}, then (3.5) is immediate. If λi>μ1\lambda_{i}>\mu_{1}, then in the λi−μ1\lambda_{i}-\mu_{1} columns indexed from μ1+1\mu_{1}+1 to λi\lambda_{i}, there are skew cells in all rows from the first to the ii-th. In each of these columns, column strictness makes the entry in the ii-th row at least ii, while the first part of the lemma makes it at most ii, so this entry has to be ii. Then there are at least λi−μ1\lambda_{i}-\mu_{1} cells filled with ii, thereby yielding (3.5). ∎

Define the rectangular partition

(ml):=(m,…,m⏟l parts).\displaystyle(m^{l}):=(\underbrace{m,\ldots,m}_{\text{$l$ parts}}).

The complete homogeneous symmetric functions hrh_{r} and the elementary symmetric functions ere_{r}, defined respectively by

hr:=s(r),er:=s(1r),\displaystyle h_{r}:=s_{(r)},\qquad\qquad e_{r}:=s_{(1^{r})}, (3.6)

are the most basic Schur functions indexed by rectangular partitions. Here we adopt the convention that h0=e0=1h_{0}=e_{0}=1 and hr=er=0h_{r}=e_{r}=0 for r<0r<0.

We also need a special shape of skew diagrams for later use. A skew diagram λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a horizontal strip if it has at most one cell in each column. We write

“λ/μ​HS\lambda/\mu\,\,\mathrm{HS}”

for this condition. In particular, this condition is equivalent to

λ1≥μ1≥λ2≥μ2≥λ3≥⋯.\displaystyle\lambda_{1}\geq\mu_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\mu_{2}\geq\lambda_{3}\geq\cdots. (3.7)

According to the product form of the Pieri rule [15, p. 339, Theorem 7.15.7],

hrsμ=∑λ:λ/μ​HS|λ|−|μ|=rsλ.\displaystyle h_{r}s_{\mu}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\colon\lambda/\mu\,\,\mathrm{HS}\\ |\lambda|-|\mu|=r\end{subarray}}s_{\lambda}. (3.8)

Also, the skew form of the Pieri rule [15, p. 340, Corollary 7.15.9] states that

sλ/(r)=∑μ:λ/μ​HS|λ|−|μ|=rsμ.\displaystyle s_{\lambda/(r)}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\colon\lambda/\mu\,\,\mathrm{HS}\\ |\lambda|-|\mu|=r\end{subarray}}s_{\mu}. (3.9)

Now we move on to the Schur positivity related to rectangular partitions.

Lemma 3.2.

Let u≥1u\geq 1 and a≥b≥1a\geq b\geq 1. Then

s(au)s(bu)−s((a+1)u)s((b−1)u)≥s0.\displaystyle s_{(a^{u})}s_{(b^{u})}-s_{((a+1)^{u})}s_{((b-1)^{u})}\geq_{s}0. (3.10)
Proof.

By (3.1),

s(au)​s(bu)−s((a+1)u)​s((b−1)u)=∑λ(c(au),(bu)λ−c((a+1)u),((b−1)u)λ)​sλ.\displaystyle s_{(a^{u})}s_{(b^{u})}-s_{((a+1)^{u})}s_{((b-1)^{u})}=\sum_{\lambda}\big(c_{(a^{u}),(b^{u})}^{\lambda}-c_{((a+1)^{u}),((b-1)^{u})}^{\lambda}\big)s_{\lambda}.

It is sufficient to show that for every partition λ\lambda,

c(au),(bu)λ−c((a+1)u),((b−1)u)λ≥0.\displaystyle c_{(a^{u}),(b^{u})}^{\lambda}-c_{((a+1)^{u}),((b-1)^{u})}^{\lambda}\geq 0. (3.11)

If ((a+1)u)⊈λ((a+1)^{u})\not\subseteq\lambda, then c((a+1)u),((b−1)u)λ=0c_{((a+1)^{u}),((b-1)^{u})}^{\lambda}=0 according to the Littlewood–Richardson rule, and hence (3.11) holds. Now assume that ((a+1)u)⊆λ((a+1)^{u})\subseteq\lambda so that λi≥a+1\lambda_{i}\geq a+1 for every index ii with 1≤i≤u1\leq i\leq u. If c((a+1)u),((b−1)u)λ=0c_{((a+1)^{u}),((b-1)^{u})}^{\lambda}=0, then we still have nothing to prove. Hence, we further assume that c((a+1)u),((b−1)u)λ>0c_{((a+1)^{u}),((b-1)^{u})}^{\lambda}>0. We claim that λu+1<a+1\lambda_{u+1}<a+1. Note that the Littlewood–Richardson rule ensures the existence of a Littlewood–Richardson tableau of shape λ/((a+1)u)\lambda/((a+1)^{u}) and type ((b−1)u)((b-1)^{u}). By column strictness and the first assertion in Lemma 3.1, we know that all cells in the ii-th row of λ/((a+1)u)\lambda/((a+1)^{u}) are filled with ii. Also, (3.5) in Lemma 3.1 tells us that λi≤(a+1)+(b−1)=a+b\lambda_{i}\leq(a+1)+(b-1)=a+b. Next, by the Littlewood–Richardson condition, we may fill the (u+1)(u+1)-th row of λ/((a+1)u)\lambda/((a+1)^{u}) with uu of multiplicity at most λu−1−λu\lambda_{u-1}-\lambda_{u}, preceded by u−1u-1 of multiplicity at most λu−2−λu−1\lambda_{u-2}-\lambda_{u-1}, and so forth, till 11 of multiplicity λ0−λ1\lambda_{0}-\lambda_{1} where λ0=a+b\lambda_{0}=a+b. Thus,

λu+1≤λ0−λu≤(a+b)−(a+1)=b−1<a+1\displaystyle\lambda_{u+1}\leq\lambda_{0}-\lambda_{u}\leq(a+b)-(a+1)=b-1<a+1

since b≤ab\leq a. Now for any Littlewood–Richardson tableau of shape λ/((a+1)u)\lambda/((a+1)^{u}) and type ((b−1)u)((b-1)^{u}), we can injectively obtain a Littlewood–Richardson tableau of shape λ/(au)\lambda/(a^{u}) and type (bu)(b^{u}) by preserving the fillings of the former tableau and then filling the (a+1)(a+1)-th column of λ/(au)\lambda/(a^{u}), which contains exactly uu cells, with 1,2,…,u1,2,\ldots,u, from top to bottom. Therefore, (3.11) is also valid in this situation. ∎

Let ω\omega be the standard involution on Λ\Lambda, defined by

ω⁡(sλ):=sλ𝖳,\displaystyle\omega(s_{\lambda}):=s_{\lambda^{\mathsf{T}}},

which preserves the Schur positivity. Since ω\omega is a ring automorphism, it is true that for any F,G∈ΛF,G\in\Lambda,

ω⁡(F​G)=ω⁡(F)​ω​(G).\displaystyle\omega(FG)=\omega(F)\omega(G). (3.12)

Also, we know from [15, p. 338, Theorem 7.15.6] that

ω⁡(sλ/μ)=sλ𝖳/μ𝖳.\displaystyle\omega(s_{\lambda/\mu})=s_{\lambda^{\mathsf{T}}/\mu^{\mathsf{T}}}. (3.13)

We then arrive at a companion to Lemma 3.2, which also appeared in [1, Remark 7.2].

Lemma 3.3.

Let u≥1u\geq 1 and a≥b≥1a\geq b\geq 1. Then

s(ua)s(ub)−s(ua+1)s(ub−1)≥s0.\displaystyle s_{(u^{a})}s_{(u^{b})}-s_{(u^{a+1})}s_{(u^{b-1})}\geq_{s}0. (3.14)
Proof.

Applying ω\omega to the left-hand side of (3.10) produces the left-hand side of (3.14), where we have used (3.12). Since ω\omega preserves the Schur positivity, the desired statement follows from Lemma 3.2. ∎

The preceding content works for generic alphabets X=(x1,x2,…)X=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots). Now let XN:=(x1,…,xN)X_{N}:=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}) be finite. The specialization map spN\operatorname{sp}_{N} sets all variables after xNx_{N} to 00, so that

spN⁡(F):=F⁡(XN).\displaystyle\operatorname{sp}_{N}(F):=F(X_{N}).

We introduce a companion operator that will be frequently utilized:

spN𝖳⁡(F):=spN⁡(ω⁡(F)).\displaystyle\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N}(F):=\operatorname{sp}_{N}\big(\omega(F)\big).

In particular, (3.12) tells us that for any F,G∈ΛF,G\in\Lambda,

spN𝖳⁡(F​G)=spN𝖳⁡(F)​spN𝖳⁡(G).\displaystyle\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N}(FG)=\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N}(F)\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N}(G). (3.15)

Finally, we define the projection onto Schur functions of width at most NN by

πN(∑λaλsλ):=∑λ:λ1≤Naλsλ.\displaystyle\pi_{N}\left(\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}s_{\lambda}\right):=\sum_{\lambda\colon\lambda_{1}\leq N}a_{\lambda}s_{\lambda}.

Let

IN:=span⁡{sλ:λ1>N}.\displaystyle I_{N}:=\operatorname{span}\{s_{\lambda}\colon\lambda_{1}>N\}.
Lemma 3.4.

The span INI_{N} is an ideal of Λ\Lambda.

Proof.

Suppose sλs_{\lambda} occurs in the Schur expansion of sμ​sνs_{\mu}s_{\nu} so that cμ,νλ>0c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}>0. According to Lemma 3.1, μ,ν⊆λ\mu,\nu\subseteq\lambda. Thus, if μ1>1\mu_{1}>1 or ν1>1\nu_{1}>1, we must have λ1>1\lambda_{1}>1. This means that multiplication of an element of InI_{n} and an arbitrary symmetric function in Λ\Lambda remains in INI_{N}, thereby confirming that INI_{N} is an ideal. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

Both spN𝖳\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N} and πN\pi_{N} annihilate all functions in INI_{N}.

Proof.

The annihilation of πN\pi_{N} follows by definition. Next, spN𝖳⁡(sλ)=sλ𝖳​(XN)\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N}(s_{\lambda})=s_{\lambda^{\mathsf{T}}}(X_{N}), which vanishes when 𝗅𝖾𝗇⁡(λ𝖳)>N\mathsf{len}(\lambda^{\mathsf{T}})>N since in this case the first column already requires more than NN distinct variables. In this case, we have λ1>N\lambda_{1}>N, yielding the annihilation of spN𝖳\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N} on INI_{N}. ∎

Lemma 3.6.

For any F∈ΛF\in\Lambda,

spN𝖳⁡(F)=spN𝖳⁡(πN​(F)).\displaystyle\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N}(F)=\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N}\big(\pi_{N}(F)\big). (3.16)

Also, spN𝖳\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N} is injective on the span of sλs_{\lambda} with λ1≤N\lambda_{1}\leq N.

Proof.

Note that

F=πN​(F)+(F−πN​(F)),\displaystyle F=\pi_{N}(F)+\big(F-\pi_{N}(F)\big),

with F−πN​(F)∈INF-\pi_{N}(F)\in I_{N}. We then use the annihilation of spN𝖳\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{N} on INI_{N} to obtain the claimed relation (3.16). For the second assertion, we only need the fact that the Schur polynomials sλ𝖳​(XN)s_{\lambda^{\mathsf{T}}}(X_{N}) with λ1≤N\lambda_{1}\leq N form a basis of symmetric polynomials in NN variables. ∎

Lemma 3.7.

For any F,G∈ΛF,G\in\Lambda,

πN​(F​G)=πN​(F​πN​(G)).\displaystyle\pi_{N}(FG)=\pi_{N}\big(F\pi_{N}(G)\big). (3.17)
Proof.

Note that

F​G=F⋅πN​(G)+F⋅(G−πN​(G)).\displaystyle FG=F\cdot\pi_{N}(G)+F\cdot\big(G-\pi_{N}(G)\big).

Here G−πN​(G)G-\pi_{N}(G) is in INI_{N}, and so is F⋅(G−πN​(G))F\cdot\big(G-\pi_{N}(G)\big) since INI_{N} is an ideal of Λ\Lambda. Applying πN\pi_{N} to both sides and using the annihilation of πN\pi_{N} on INI_{N}, the claimed relation follows. ∎

Finally, we show how Schur functions are connected with dd-Hoggatt numbers and their qq-analogs. To begin with, we specify two alphabets:

QN:=(1,q,…,qN−1),1N:=(1,1,…,1⏟N copies).\displaystyle Q_{N}:=(1,q,\ldots,q^{N-1}),\qquad\qquad 1_{N}:=(\underbrace{1,1,\ldots,1}_{\text{$N$ copies}}).
Lemma 3.8.

We have

s(dk)​(Qn)=⟨nk⟩q(d).\displaystyle s_{(d^{k})}(Q_{n})={\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}^{(d)}. (3.18)

In particular,

s(dk)​(1n)=⟨nk⟩(d).\displaystyle s_{(d^{k})}(1_{n})={\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}^{(d)}. (3.19)
Proof.

By the hook-content formula [15, p. 374, Theorem 7.21.2],

s(dk)​(Qn)=qd​(k2)​∏i=1k∏j=1d[n+j−i]q[d+k−i−j−1]q=qd​(k2)​∏j=0d−1∏i=1k[n−k+i+j]q[i+j]q.\displaystyle s_{(d^{k})}(Q_{n})=q^{d\binom{k}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{d}\frac{[n+j-i]_{q}}{[d+k-i-j-1]_{q}}=q^{d\binom{k}{2}}\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{[n-k+i+j]_{q}}{[i+j]_{q}}.

To get the last equality, we have interchanged the products, and then made the change of indices (i,j)↦(k−i+1,j+1)(i,j)\mapsto(k-i+1,j+1) for the numerator and (i,j)↦(k−i+1,d−j)(i,j)\mapsto(k-i+1,d-j) for the denominator. Now

s(dk)​(Qn)=qd​(k2)​∏j=0d−1[n+jk]q[k+jk]q,\displaystyle s_{(d^{k})}(Q_{n})=q^{d\binom{k}{2}}\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n+j}{k}}_{q}}{{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{k+j}{k}}_{q}},

thereby giving (3.18) by recalling (1.2). For (3.19), we only need the specialization at q=1q=1. ∎

Lemma 3.9.

We have, for r≥0r\geq 0,

s(rk)​(Qd+k)=q(r−d)​(k2)​⟨k+rk⟩q(d).\displaystyle s_{(r^{k})}(Q_{d+k})=q^{(r-d)\binom{k}{2}}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{k+r}{k}}_{q}^{(d)}. (3.20)
Proof.

If r=0r=0, then both sides of (3.20) are 11. Now assume r≥1r\geq 1. We have shown in the preceding proof that

s(rk)​(Qd+k)=qr​(k2)​∏i=1k∏j=0r−1[d+i+j]q[i+j]q.\displaystyle s_{(r^{k})}(Q_{d+k})=q^{r\binom{k}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{[d+i+j]_{q}}{[i+j]_{q}}.

Note that for each ii,

∏j=0r−1[d+i+j]q[i+j]q=∏j=0d−1[r+i+j]q[i+j]q.\displaystyle\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{[d+i+j]_{q}}{[i+j]_{q}}=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{[r+i+j]_{q}}{[i+j]_{q}}.

Thus,

s(rk)​(Qd+k)=qr​(k2)​∏i=1k∏j=0d−1[r+i+j]q[i+j]q=qr​(k2)​∏j=0d−1[k+r+jk]q[k+jk]q,\displaystyle s_{(r^{k})}(Q_{d+k})=q^{r\binom{k}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{[r+i+j]_{q}}{[i+j]_{q}}=q^{r\binom{k}{2}}\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{k+r+j}{k}}_{q}}{{\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{k+j}{k}}_{q}},

which yields (3.20) in light of (1.2). ∎

4. Strong qq-log-concavity of the qq-analog of dd-Hoggatt numbers

4.1. Proof of Theorem 1.3

Let k,lk,l be such that 0<l≤k<n0<l\leq k<n. It follows from (3.18) that

⟨nk⟩q​⟨nl⟩q−⟨nk+1⟩q​⟨nl−1⟩q=s(dk)​(Qn)​s(dl)​(Qn)−s(dk+1)​(Qn)​s(dl−1)​(Qn).\displaystyle{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{l}}_{q}-{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k+1}}_{q}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{l-1}}_{q}=s_{(d^{k})}(Q_{n})s_{(d^{l})}(Q_{n})-s_{(d^{k+1})}(Q_{n})s_{(d^{l-1})}(Q_{n}).

Now by Lemma 3.3, the right-hand side of the above is in ℕ⁡[q]\mathbb{N}[q], thereby implying the strong qq-log-concavity of (⟨nk⟩q)0≤k≤n\big({\textstyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}\big)_{0\leq k\leq n}.

4.2. Proof of Theorem 1.4

Let m,nm,n be such that n≥m>kn\geq m>k. If k=0k=0, we have

⟨nk⟩q​⟨mk⟩q−⟨n+1k⟩q​⟨m−1k⟩q=0.\displaystyle{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{m}{k}}_{q}-{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+1}{k}}_{q}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{m-1}{k}}_{q}=0.

Now assume k≥1k\geq 1. It follows from (3.20) that

⟨nk⟩q​⟨mk⟩q−⟨n+1k⟩q​⟨m−1k⟩q\displaystyle{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{m}{k}}_{q}-{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n+1}{k}}_{q}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{m-1}{k}}_{q}
=q(2​d−n†−m†)​(k2)​(s(n†k)​(Qd+k)​s(m†k)​(Qd+k)−s((n†+1)k)​(Qd+k)​s((m†−1)k)​(Qd+k)),\displaystyle\ \ =q^{(2d-n_{\dagger}-m_{\dagger})\binom{k}{2}}\big(s_{(n_{\dagger}^{k})}(Q_{d+k})s_{(m_{\dagger}^{k})}(Q_{d+k})-s_{((n_{\dagger}+1)^{k})}(Q_{d+k})s_{((m_{\dagger}-1)^{k})}(Q_{d+k})\big),

where m†:=m−km_{\dagger}:=m-k and n†:=n−kn_{\dagger}:=n-k. Now by Lemma 3.2, the second factor on the right-hand side of the above is in ℕ⁡[q]\mathbb{N}[q]. Noting that the left-hand side is in ℤ⁡[q]\mathbb{Z}[q] by definition, we conclude that the left-hand side must be in ℕ⁡[q]\mathbb{N}[q] because multiplying by the prefactor q(2​d−n†−m†)​(k2)q^{(2d-n_{\dagger}-m_{\dagger})\binom{k}{2}} does not affect the signs of the coefficients. We then arrive at the strong qq-log-concavity of (⟨nk⟩q)n≥k\big({\textstyle\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}}_{q}\big)_{n\geq k}.

5. Schur positivity of an auxiliary family of functions

In the next two sections, we set two types of partitions:

Rl:=(d,…,d⏟l parts),Pl(j):=(d,…,d⏟l parts,j),\displaystyle R_{l}:=(\underbrace{d,\ldots,d}_{\text{$l$ parts}}),\qquad\qquad P_{l}^{(j)}:=(\underbrace{d,\ldots,d}_{\text{$l$ parts}},j),

where 0≤j≤d0\leq j\leq d. Note that Rl=Pl(0)R_{l}=P_{l}^{(0)} and Rl+1=Pl(d)R_{l+1}=P_{l}^{(d)}. We adopt the convention that all expressions containing RlR_{l} or Pl(j)P_{l}^{(j)} with l<0l<0 are assumed to be 00. For a partition β\beta and an integer t≥0t\geq 0, define the auxiliary functions

Φt,jβ:=∑u+v=t(sPu(j)/β​sRv−sRu/β​sPv(j)).\displaystyle\Phi_{t,j}^{\beta}:=\sum_{u+v=t}\big(s_{P_{u}^{(j)}/\beta}s_{R_{v}}-s_{R_{u}/\beta}s_{P_{v}^{(j)}}\big). (5.1)

The purpose of this section is to establish the following Schur positivity property.

Theorem 5.1.

For any jj and tt with 1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1 and t≥0t\geq 0, and any partition β\beta,

Φt,jβ≥s0.\displaystyle\Phi_{t,j}^{\beta}\geq_{s}0. (5.2)

We shall prove this theorem by induction on tt. When t=0t=0,

Φ0,jβ={s(j)/β,if β≠∅,0,if β=∅,\displaystyle\Phi_{0,j}^{\beta}=\begin{cases}s_{(j)/\beta},&\text{if $\beta\neq\varnothing$},\\ 0,&\text{if $\beta=\varnothing$},\end{cases}

which is clearly Schur positive. Now assume that the theorem is true for 0,…,t−10,\ldots,t-1 with t≥1t\geq 1. It suffices to show that the coefficients in the Schur expansion of Φt,jβ\Phi_{t,j}^{\beta} satisfy

[sα]​Φt,jβ≥0\displaystyle[s_{\alpha}]\Phi_{t,j}^{\beta}\geq 0 (5.3)

for every partition α\alpha.

Now there are two cases, depending on whether α\alpha contains parts of size dd or not. To facilitate our analysis, we introduce a linear map

Δd:Λ→Λsλ↦sd∪λ\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{cccc}\Delta_{d}\colon&\Lambda&\to&\Lambda\\ &s_{\lambda}&\mapsto&s_{d\cup\lambda}\end{array}

with d∪λd\cup\lambda the partition derived by adjoining a part of size dd in λ\lambda and rearranging the parts in weakly decreasing order. We will see how adjoining a part dd behaves after the projection πd\pi_{d}.

Lemma 5.2.

For any F,G∈ΛF,G\in\Lambda,

πd​(F​Δd​(G))=Δd​(πd​(F​G)).\displaystyle\pi_{d}\big(F\Delta_{d}(G)\big)=\Delta_{d}\big(\pi_{d}(FG)\big). (5.4)
Proof.

We start with an auxiliary relation that for any F∈ΛF\in\Lambda,

spd𝖳⁡(Δd​(πd​(F)))=ed​(Xd)​spd𝖳⁡(F).\displaystyle\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\Delta_{d}(\pi_{d}(F))\big)=e_{d}(X_{d})\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(F). (5.5)

By the linearity of the operators, it suffices to prove (5.5) for every Schur polynomial sλs_{\lambda}. If λ1>d\lambda_{1}>d, we have πd​(sλ)=0\pi_{d}(s_{\lambda})=0, and further spd𝖳⁡(sλ)=spd𝖳⁡(πd​(sλ))=0\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(s_{\lambda})=\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\pi_{d}(s_{\lambda})\big)=0 by (3.16), so that both sides of (5.5) vanishes. Now assume λ1≤d\lambda_{1}\leq d. We have

spd𝖳⁡(Δd​(πd​(sλ)))=spd𝖳⁡(sd∪λ)=s(d∪λ)𝖳​(Xd).\displaystyle\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\Delta_{d}(\pi_{d}(s_{\lambda}))\big)=\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(s_{d\cup\lambda})=s_{(d\cup\lambda)^{\mathsf{T}}}(X_{d}).

Note that in dd variables, there is only one way to fill the first column of (d∪λ)𝖳(d\cup\lambda)^{\mathsf{T}}, namely, by filling in 11 through nn from top to bottom. By doing so, we factor out ed​(Xd)=s(1d)​(Xd)e_{d}(X_{d})=s_{(1^{d})}(X_{d}) and spd𝖳⁡(sλ)\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(s_{\lambda}), and hence arrive at the desired relation (5.5) for F=sλF=s_{\lambda},

spd𝖳⁡(Δd​(πd​(sλ)))=ed​(Xd)​spd𝖳⁡(sλ).\displaystyle\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\Delta_{d}(\pi_{d}(s_{\lambda}))\big)=e_{d}(X_{d})\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(s_{\lambda}).

Now moving back to (5.4), we see that both sides are in the span of sλs_{\lambda} with λ1≤d\lambda_{1}\leq d. Using (5.5) twice and recalling (3.15),

spd𝖳⁡(Δd​(πd​(F​G)))\displaystyle\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\Delta_{d}(\pi_{d}(FG))\big) =ed​(Xd)​spd𝖳⁡(F​G)\displaystyle=e_{d}(X_{d})\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(FG)
=ed​(Xd)​spd𝖳⁡(F)​spd𝖳⁡(G)\displaystyle=e_{d}(X_{d})\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(F)\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(G)
=spd𝖳⁡(F)​spd𝖳⁡(Δd​(πd​(G))).\displaystyle=\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(F)\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\Delta_{d}(\pi_{d}(G))\big).

It is clear that G−πd​(G)G-\pi_{d}(G) is in IdI_{d}, and so is Δd​(G)−Δd​(πd​(G))\Delta_{d}(G)-\Delta_{d}(\pi_{d}(G)). By Lemma 3.5, this difference is annihilated by spd𝖳\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}. Therefore, spd𝖳⁡(Δd​(πd​(G)))=spd𝖳⁡(Δd​(G))\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\Delta_{d}(\pi_{d}(G))\big)=\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\Delta_{d}(G)\big), so that

spd𝖳⁡(Δd​(πd​(F​G)))=spd𝖳⁡(F)​spd𝖳⁡(Δd​(G))=spd𝖳⁡(F​Δd​(G))=spd𝖳⁡(πd​(F​Δd​(G))),\displaystyle\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\Delta_{d}(\pi_{d}(FG))\big)=\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}(F)\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\Delta_{d}(G)\big)=\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(F\Delta_{d}(G)\big)=\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d}\big(\pi_{d}(F\Delta_{d}(G))\big),

where we have used (3.15) for the second equality and (3.16) for the last equality. Now the claimed identity (5.4) follows from the injectivity of spd𝖳\operatorname{sp}^{\mathsf{T}}_{d} in Lemma 3.6. ∎

In the following two subsections, we fix jj with 1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1 and put

d′:=d−j.\displaystyle d^{\prime}:=d-j.

Before analyzing the two cases of α\alpha individually, we record a useful fact about rotated skew diagrams inside a rectangular partition. It is known that the skew Schur function of a diagram is unchanged when the diagram is rotated through 180180 degrees. This is [15, p. 467, Exerise 7.56(a)] with its proof given on [15, p. 516].

Lemma 5.3.

Let β⊆Ru=(du)\beta\subseteq R_{u}=(d^{u}) so that 𝗅𝖾𝗇⁡(β)≤u\mathsf{len}(\beta)\leq u, and define

κ:=(d−βu,d−βu−1,…,d−β1).\displaystyle\kappa:=(d-\beta_{u},d-\beta_{u-1},\ldots,d-\beta_{1}).

Then

sRu/β=sκ,sRu+1/β=sd∪κ,sPu(j)/β=s(d∪κ)/(d′).\displaystyle s_{R_{u}/\beta}=s_{\kappa},\qquad s_{R_{u+1}/\beta}=s_{d\cup\kappa},\qquad s_{P_{u}^{(j)}/\beta}=s_{(d\cup\kappa)/(d^{\prime})}. (5.6)

Since β\beta is inside RuR_{u}, it is also inside Ru+1R_{u+1} and Pu(j)P_{u}^{(j)}. Note that Ru/βR_{u}/\beta is obtained by rotating κ\kappa through 180180 degrees, and hence sRu/β=sκs_{R_{u}/\beta}=s_{\kappa}. The remaining two relations can be derived in the same way. ∎

Finally, we introduce two auxiliary coefficients for u,v≥0u,v\geq 0 and an arbitrary partition λ\lambda:

Au,v​(λ):=⟨sλ,sPu(j)/β​sRv⟩≥0,Bu,v​(λ):=⟨sλ,sRu/β​sPv(j)⟩≥0,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} A_{u,v}(\lambda)&:=\big\langle s_{\lambda},s_{P_{u}^{(j)}/\beta}s_{R_{v}}\big\rangle\geq 0,\\ B_{u,v}(\lambda)&:=\big\langle s_{\lambda},s_{R_{u}/\beta}s_{P_{v}^{(j)}}\big\rangle\geq 0,\end{aligned} (5.7)

with the nonnegativity coming from the Schur positivity of sPu(j)/β​sRvs_{P_{u}^{(j)}/\beta}s_{R_{v}} and sRu/β​sPv(j)s_{R_{u}/\beta}s_{P_{v}^{(j)}}. In addition, we adopt the convention that Au,v​(λ)=Bu,v​(λ)=0A_{u,v}(\lambda)=B_{u,v}(\lambda)=0 if u<0u<0 or v<0v<0.

Lemma 5.4.

For any partition λ\lambda with pλ:=#⁡{i:λi>d}p_{\lambda}:=\#\{i\colon\lambda_{i}>d\}, we have

{Au,v​(λ)=0,if v<pλ,Bu,v​(λ)=0,if v<pλ−1.\displaystyle\begin{cases}A_{u,v}(\lambda)=0,&\text{if $v<p_{\lambda}$},\\ B_{u,v}(\lambda)=0,&\text{if $v<p_{\lambda}-1$}.\end{cases} (5.8)
Proof.

By (3.2) and (3.1),

sPu(j)/β​sRv=∑μcμ,βPu(j)​sμ​sRv=∑λ∑μcμ,βPu(j)​cμ,Rvλ​sλ,\displaystyle s_{P_{u}^{(j)}/\beta}s_{R_{v}}=\sum_{\mu}c_{\mu,\beta}^{P_{u}^{(j)}}s_{\mu}s_{R_{v}}=\sum_{\lambda}\sum_{\mu}c_{\mu,\beta}^{P_{u}^{(j)}}c_{\mu,R_{v}}^{\lambda}s_{\lambda},

so that

Au,v​(λ)=∑μcμ,βPu(j)​cμ,Rvλ.\displaystyle A_{u,v}(\lambda)=\sum_{\mu}c_{\mu,\beta}^{P_{u}^{(j)}}c_{\mu,R_{v}}^{\lambda}. (5.9)

To ensure Au,v​(λ)>0A_{u,v}(\lambda)>0, we need to find a certain μ\mu such that cμ,βPu(j)>0c_{\mu,\beta}^{P_{u}^{(j)}}>0 and cμ,Rvλ>0c_{\mu,R_{v}}^{\lambda}>0 hold simultaneously. For the first inequality, Lemma 3.1 tells us that μ⊆Pu(j)\mu\subseteq P_{u}^{(j)} so that μ1≤d\mu_{1}\leq d. For the second inequality, we use (3.5) in Lemma 3.1 to get λv+1≤μ1+(Rv)v+1=μ1\lambda_{v+1}\leq\mu_{1}+(R_{v})_{v+1}=\mu_{1}. Thus, λv+1≤d\lambda_{v+1}\leq d. However, if v<pλv<p_{\lambda}, then λv+1>d\lambda_{v+1}>d by the definition of pλp_{\lambda}. This produces a contradiction, and hence Au,v​(λ)=0A_{u,v}(\lambda)=0 when v<pλv<p_{\lambda}. For the second statement involving Bu,v​(λ)B_{u,v}(\lambda), we apply a similar analysis but this time to λv+2\lambda_{v+2}. ∎

5.1. The partition α\alpha contains parts of size dd

Throughout this subsection, since α\alpha contains parts of size dd, we always write it as

α:=(d+τ1,…,d+τp,d,η1,…,ηr),\displaystyle\alpha:=(d+\tau_{1},\ldots,d+\tau_{p},d,\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{r}), (5.10)

where τ:=(τ1,…,τp)\tau:=(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{p}) is a partition with exactly pp positive parts, and η:=(η1,…,ηr)\eta:=(\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{r}) is a partition with width η1≤d\eta_{1}\leq d. Define

Lemma 5.5.

For any partition λ\lambda with λ1≤d\lambda_{1}\leq d,

⟨sλ,sα/Pp(j)⟩=⟨sλ/(d′),sα−/Rp⟩.\displaystyle\big\langle s_{\lambda},s_{\alpha/P_{p}^{(j)}}\big\rangle=\big\langle s_{\lambda/(d^{\prime})},s_{\alpha^{-}/R_{p}}\big\rangle. (5.11)

s(d∪η)/(j)=∑ξ:(d∪η)/ξ​HS|d∪η|−|ξ|=jsξ.\displaystyle s_{(d\cup\eta)/(j)}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\xi\colon(d\cup\eta)/\xi\,\,\mathrm{HS}\\ |d\cup\eta|-|\xi|=j\end{subarray}}s_{\xi}.

We then derive that

5.2. The partition α\alpha contains no part of size dd

Throughout this subsection, since α\alpha does not contain any part of size dd, we always write it as

Lemma 5.10.

hd′sτ−sT=∑ζ:ζ/τ​HS|ζ|−|τ|=d′𝗅𝖾𝗇⁡(ζ)=p+1sζ.\displaystyle h_{d^{\prime}}s_{\tau}-s_{T}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\zeta\colon\zeta/\tau\,\,\mathrm{HS}\\ |\zeta|-|\tau|=d^{\prime}\\ \mathsf{len}(\zeta)=p+1\end{subarray}}s_{\zeta}. (5.22)

sT=∑ζ:ζ/τ​HS|ζ|−|τ|=d′𝗅𝖾𝗇⁡(ζ)≤psζ,\displaystyle s_{T}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\zeta\colon\zeta/\tau\,\,\mathrm{HS}\\ |\zeta|-|\tau|=d^{\prime}\\ \mathsf{len}(\zeta)\leq p\end{subarray}}s_{\zeta},

In the next two lemmas, we shall use the dual Jacobi–Trudi formula [15, p. 344, Corollary 7.16.2], which states that for two partitions λ\lambda and μ\mu with length at most ll such that μ⊆λ\mu\subseteq\lambda,

s(λ/μ)𝖳​(XN)=det1≤a,b≤l​(eλa−μb−a+b​(XN)).\displaystyle s_{(\lambda/\mu)^{\mathsf{T}}}(X_{N})=\underset{1\leq a,b\leq l}{\det}\big(e_{\lambda_{a}-\mu_{b}-a+b}(X_{N})\big). (5.23)

Lemma 5.12.

We have

The final piece of the ingredients we need is a simplification of [sα]​Φt,jβ[s_{\alpha}]\Phi_{t,j}^{\beta} for our choice of α\alpha.

Lemma 5.14.

We have

[sα]​Φt,jβ={At−p,p​(α)−Bt−p,p​(α)−Bt−p+1,p−1​(α),if t≥p,0,if t<p.\displaystyle[s_{\alpha}]\Phi_{t,j}^{\beta}=\begin{cases}A_{t-p,p}(\alpha)-B_{t-p,p}(\alpha)-B_{t-p+1,p-1}(\alpha),&\text{if $t\geq p$},\\ 0,&\text{if $t<p$}.\end{cases} (5.27)

Recalling (5.7),

According to (5.9), if At−v,v​(α)>0A_{t-v,v}(\alpha)>0, then we must have Rv⊆αR_{v}\subseteq\alpha, so that αv≥d\alpha_{v}\geq d. Since dd does not appear in α\alpha, we indeed have αv>d\alpha_{v}>d, which implies that v≤pv\leq p. By the relation for AA in (5.8),

Similarly, if Bt−v,v​(α)>0B_{t-v,v}(\alpha)>0, we need Pv(j)⊆αP_{v}^{(j)}\subseteq\alpha, which in the same way, gives v≤pv\leq p. By the relation for BB in (5.8),

Hence,

[sα]​Φt,jβ=At−p,p​(α)−Bt−p,p​(α)−Bt−p+1,p−1​(α).\displaystyle[s_{\alpha}]\Phi_{t,j}^{\beta}=A_{t-p,p}(\alpha)-B_{t-p,p}(\alpha)-B_{t-p+1,p-1}(\alpha).

Now (5.27) is plain when t≥pt\geq p or t≤p−2t\leq p-2. For the last case t=p−1t=p-1, we have

[sα]​Φp−1,jβ=−B0,p−1​(α)=−⟨sα,s∅/β​sPp−1(j)⟩.\displaystyle[s_{\alpha}]\Phi_{p-1,j}^{\beta}=-B_{0,p-1}(\alpha)=-\big\langle s_{\alpha},s_{\varnothing/\beta}s_{P_{p-1}^{(j)}}\big\rangle.

If β≠∅\beta\neq\varnothing, then the skew diagram ∅/β\varnothing/\beta is invalid so that s∅/β=0s_{\varnothing/\beta}=0 and hence that [sα]​Φp−1,jβ=0[s_{\alpha}]\Phi_{p-1,j}^{\beta}=0. If β=∅\beta=\varnothing, then [sα]​Φp−1,j∅=−⟨sα,sPp−1(j)⟩[s_{\alpha}]\Phi_{p-1,j}^{\varnothing}=-\big\langle s_{\alpha},s_{P_{p-1}^{(j)}}\big\rangle. Note that α≠Pp−1(j)\alpha\neq P_{p-1}^{(j)}; otherwise, α\alpha has a part of size dd because p−1=t≥1p-1=t\geq 1 by the inductive assumption, but this violates our requirement for α\alpha. Hence, [sα]​Φp−1,j∅[s_{\alpha}]\Phi_{p-1,j}^{\varnothing} still vanishes. ∎

Unlike Theorem 5.7 for the first case of α\alpha in the preceding subsection, this time we confirm (5.3) directly.

Theorem 5.15.

Let α\alpha be a partition containing no part of size dd. Then

[sα]​Φt,jβ≥0.\displaystyle[s_{\alpha}]\Phi_{t,j}^{\beta}\geq 0. (5.28)
Proof.

It suffices to assume t≥pt\geq p in light of (5.27). By the same arguments as we show (5.12) and (5.13), it is true that

sα/Rp=sτ​sρ,\displaystyle s_{\alpha/R_{p}}=s_{\tau}s_{\rho},

and

sα/Pp(j)=sτ​sρ/(j).\displaystyle s_{\alpha/P_{p}^{(j)}}=s_{\tau}s_{\rho/(j)}.

We also recall from the definition of the skew diagram DD that

sα/Pp−1(j)=sD.\displaystyle s_{\alpha/P_{p-1}^{(j)}}=s_{D}.

For convenience, write

t′:=t−p.\displaystyle t^{\prime}:=t-p.

Note that

Rt′⊆Pt′(j)⊆Rt′+1.\displaystyle R_{t^{\prime}}\subseteq P_{t^{\prime}}^{(j)}\subseteq R_{t^{\prime}+1}.

We then have four cases of β\beta.

Case 1: β⊆Rt′\beta\subseteq R_{t^{\prime}}. Let κ:=(d−βt′,…,d−β1)\kappa:=(d-\beta_{t^{\prime}},\ldots,d-\beta_{1}) be the rotated completement of β\beta in Rt′R_{t^{\prime}} and put κ+:=d∪κ\kappa^{+}:=d\cup\kappa. By (5.6),

sRt′/β=sκ,sRt′+1/β=sκ+,sPt′(j)/β=sκ+/(d′).\displaystyle s_{R_{t^{\prime}}/\beta}=s_{\kappa},\qquad s_{R_{t^{\prime}+1}/\beta}=s_{\kappa^{+}},\qquad s_{P_{t^{\prime}}^{(j)}/\beta}=s_{\kappa^{+}/(d^{\prime})}.

6. Strong qq-log-convexity of dd-Hoggatt polynomials

For any alphabet XX, define a formal power series in Λ⁡[[q]]\Lambda[[q]]:

HX​(q)=HX(d)​(q):=∑k≥0sRk​(X)​qk.\displaystyle\mydutchcal{H}_{X}(q)=\mydutchcal{H}_{X}^{(d)}(q):=\sum_{k\geq 0}s_{R_{k}}(X)q^{k}. (6.1)
Lemma 6.1.

We have

H1N(d)​(q)=HN(d)​(q).\displaystyle\mydutchcal{H}_{1_{N}}^{(d)}(q)=H_{N}^{(d)}(q). (6.2)
Proof.

Note that sRk​(1N)=0s_{R_{k}}(1_{N})=0 for all k>Nk>N because in these cases RkR_{k} has more than NN rows and hence requires more than NN variables to ensure nonvanishing. Therefore,

H1N​(q)=∑k=0NsRk​(1N)​qk=∑k=0N⟨Nk⟩​qk=HN​(q),\displaystyle\mydutchcal{H}_{1_{N}}(q)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}s_{R_{k}}(1_{N})q^{k}=\sum_{k=0}^{N}{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{N}{k}}q^{k}=H_{N}(q),

where we have used (3.19). ∎

Let XN=(x1,…,xN)X_{N}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}) and YM=(y1,…,yM)Y_{M}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{M}) be two alphabets. Denote

XN⊕YM:=(x1,…,xN,y1,…,yM).\displaystyle X_{N}\oplus Y_{M}:=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N},y_{1},\ldots,y_{M}).

By separating, in a semistandard tableau of shape λ\lambda, the cells whose entries refer to variables in XNX_{N} and from those whose entries refer to variables in YMY_{M}, we have

sλ​(XN⊕YM)=∑μ⊆λsμ​(XN)​sλ/μ​(YM).\displaystyle s_{\lambda}(X_{N}\oplus Y_{M})=\sum_{\mu\subseteq\lambda}s_{\mu}(X_{N})s_{\lambda/\mu}(Y_{M}). (6.3)

In the sequel, we treat a single variable zz as an alphabet (z)(z).

Lemma 6.2.

For k≥0k\geq 0,

sRk​(XN⊕z)=∑j=0dsPk−1(j)​(XN)​zd−j.\displaystyle s_{R_{k}}(X_{N}\oplus z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}s_{P_{k-1}^{(j)}}(X_{N})z^{d-j}. (6.4)
Proof.

Note that

sλ/μ​(z)={z|λ|−|μ|,if λ/μ is a horizontal strip,0,otherwise.\displaystyle s_{\lambda/\mu}(z)=\begin{cases}z^{|\lambda|-|\mu|},&\text{if $\lambda/\mu$ is a horizontal strip},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

By (6.3), we have

sRk(XN⊕z)=∑μ:Rk/μ​HSsμ(XN)zd​k−|μ|.\displaystyle s_{R_{k}}(X_{N}\oplus z)=\sum_{\mu\colon R_{k}/\mu\,\,\mathrm{HS}}s_{\mu}(X_{N})z^{dk-|\mu|}.

Since Rk/μR_{k}/\mu is a horizontal strip if and only if μ=Pk−1(j)\mu=P_{k-1}^{(j)} for a certain jj with 0≤j≤d0\leq j\leq d. The desired identity follows. ∎

Our next result is related to the auxiliary functions Φ\Phi defined in (5.1).

Lemma 6.3.

Let AA and BB be disjoint alphabets and put X=A⊕BX=A\oplus B. Then

HX⊕z​(q)​HB​(q)−HX​(q)​HB⊕z​(q)=∑r≥1qr​∑j=1d−1zd−j​∑βsβ​(A)​Φr−1,jβ​(B).\displaystyle\mydutchcal{H}_{X\oplus z}(q)\mydutchcal{H}_{B}(q)-\mydutchcal{H}_{X}(q)\mydutchcal{H}_{B\oplus z}(q)=\sum_{r\geq 1}q^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}z^{d-j}\sum_{\beta}s_{\beta}(A)\Phi_{r-1,j}^{\beta}(B). (6.5)
Proof.

The coefficient of q0q^{0} in HX⊕z​(q)​HB​(q)−HX​(q)​HB⊕z​(q)\mydutchcal{H}_{X\oplus z}(q)\mydutchcal{H}_{B}(q)-\mydutchcal{H}_{X}(q)\mydutchcal{H}_{B\oplus z}(q) is 1−1=01-1=0. For r≥1r\geq 1, the coefficient of qrq^{r} is

cr:=∑k+l=r(sRk​(X⊕z)​sRl​(B)−sRk​(X)​sRl​(B⊕z)).\displaystyle c_{r}:=\sum_{k+l=r}\big(s_{R_{k}}(X\oplus z)s_{R_{l}}(B)-s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B\oplus z)\big). (6.6)

Applying Lemma 6.2, we have

cr=∑j=0dzd−j​∑k+l=r(sPk−1(j)​(X)​sRl​(B)−sRk​(X)​sPl−1(j)​(B)).\displaystyle c_{r}=\sum_{j=0}^{d}z^{d-j}\sum_{k+l=r}\big(s_{P_{k-1}^{(j)}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B)-s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{P_{l-1}^{(j)}}(B)\big).

When j=0j=0, we have

∑k+l=r(sPk−1(0)​(X)​sRl​(B)−sRk​(X)​sPl−1(0)​(B))\displaystyle\sum_{k+l=r}\big(s_{P_{k-1}^{(0)}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B)-s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{P_{l-1}^{(0)}}(B)\big)
=∑k+l=r(sRk−1​(X)​sRl​(B)−sRk​(X)​sRl−1​(B))\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{k+l=r}\big(s_{R_{k-1}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B)-s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{R_{l-1}}(B)\big)
=∑k+l=r−1(sRk​(X)​sRl​(B)−sRk​(X)​sRl​(B))=0.\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{k+l=r-1}\big(s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B)-s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B)\big)=0.

When j=dj=d, we have

∑k+l=r(sPk−1(d)​(X)​sRl​(B)−sRk​(X)​sPl−1(d)​(B))\displaystyle\sum_{k+l=r}\big(s_{P_{k-1}^{(d)}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B)-s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{P_{l-1}^{(d)}}(B)\big)
=∑k+l=r(sRk​(X)​sRl​(B)−sRk​(X)​sRl​(B))=0.\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{k+l=r}\big(s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B)-s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B)\big)=0.

Thus,

cr=∑j=1d−1zd−j​∑k+l=r−1(sPk(j)​(X)​sRl​(B)−sRk​(X)​sPl(j)​(B)).\displaystyle c_{r}=\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}z^{d-j}\sum_{k+l=r-1}\big(s_{P_{k}^{(j)}}(X)s_{R_{l}}(B)-s_{R_{k}}(X)s_{P_{l}^{(j)}}(B)\big).

Recalling that X=A⊕BX=A\oplus B, we apply (6.3) and obtain

sPk(j)​(X)=sPk(j)​(A⊕B)=∑βsβ​(A)​sPk(j)/β​(B),\displaystyle s_{P_{k}^{(j)}}(X)=s_{P_{k}^{(j)}}(A\oplus B)=\sum_{\beta}s_{\beta}(A)s_{P_{k}^{(j)}/\beta}(B),

and

sRk​(X)=sRk​(A⊕B)=∑βsβ​(A)​sRk/β​(B).\displaystyle s_{R_{k}}(X)=s_{R_{k}}(A\oplus B)=\sum_{\beta}s_{\beta}(A)s_{R_{k}/\beta}(B).

It follows that

cr\displaystyle c_{r} =∑j=1d−1zd−j​∑βsβ​(A)​∑k+l=r−1(sPk(j)/β​(B)​sRl​(B)−sRk/β​(B)​sPl(j)​(B))\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}z^{d-j}\sum_{\beta}s_{\beta}(A)\sum_{k+l=r-1}\big(s_{P_{k}^{(j)}/\beta}(B)s_{R_{l}}(B)-s_{R_{k}/\beta}(B)s_{P_{l}^{(j)}}(B)\big)
=∑j=1d−1zd−j​∑βsβ​(A)​Φr−1,jβ​(B),\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}z^{d-j}\sum_{\beta}s_{\beta}(A)\Phi_{r-1,j}^{\beta}(B),

as desired. ∎

Now we are in a position to finalize the proof of Theorem 1.2.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Let n≥m≥1n\geq m\geq 1. We set A=1n−m+1A=1_{n-m+1} and B=1m−1B=1_{m-1} so that X=1nX=1_{n}. Also, set z=1z=1. Then Lemma 6.1 tells us that

Hn+1​(q)​Hm−1​(q)−Hn​(q)​Hm​(q)=HX⊕z​(q)​HB​(q)−HX​(q)​HB⊕z​(q).\displaystyle H_{n+1}(q)H_{m-1}(q)-H_{n}(q)H_{m}(q)=\mydutchcal{H}_{X\oplus z}(q)\mydutchcal{H}_{B}(q)-\mydutchcal{H}_{X}(q)\mydutchcal{H}_{B\oplus z}(q).

Since Φr−1,jβ\Phi_{r-1,j}^{\beta} is Schur positive for every jj with 1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1 according to Theorem 5.1, we conclude from (6.5) that the above is in ℕ⁡[q]\mathbb{N}[q], thereby implying the strong qq-log-convexity of (Hn​(q))n≥0(H_{n}(q))_{n\geq 0}. ∎
